slides.heading: Back to the Moon
slides.text: In April 1970, Apollo 13 set off to be the third mission to land people on the Moon. Its landing spot was a hilly area called Fra Mauro.

image.alt: The Apollo 13 mission emblem: three horses racing towards the Moon

slides.credit: Image: NASA · The Apollo 13 emblem. Its motto means 'From the Moon, knowledge'.

slides.heading: The crew
slides.text: The crew: Commander Jim Lovell, Command Module Pilot Jack Swigert, and Lunar Module Pilot Fred Haise.

image.alt: The three Apollo 13 astronauts in their spacesuits

slides.credit: Photo: NASA · Lovell, Swigert and Haise

slides.heading: A last-minute swap
slides.text: Ken Mattingly had trained for months to fly as Command Module Pilot. But three days before launch, doctors worried he might catch German measles, so his backup, Jack Swigert, took his place. Mattingly never got sick, and he became a hero on the ground.

slides.heading: Odyssey and Aquarius
slides.text: Apollo 13 had two spaceships: Odyssey, the command and service module, and Aquarius, the lunar module that would land on the Moon.

slides.heading: Liftoff!
slides.text: Apollo 13 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center in Florida at 13:13 Houston time. Watch NASA's film of the launch!
slides.speak: Apollo 13 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center in Florida at thirteen thirteen, Houston time. Watch NASA's film of the launch!

slides.heading: Your mission
slides.text: Train like Jack Swigert, meet the spaceship and fly towards the Moon. It's supposed to be a normal mission... but Apollo 13 will become one of the most famous rescues in history!

intro: Jack Swigert had only a few days to get ready! He trained in the simulator, a copy of the spaceship here on Earth.
simulator.resultText: Great memory! Astronauts practise every step in simulators until they know it by heart. Soon, all that practice would help save the crew.

watchTask.title: Watch the lights!
watchTask.help: Remember the order the switches light up in.

copyTask.title: Your turn!
copyTask.help: Press the switches in the same order.

stackReveal.title: Odyssey & Aquarius
stackReveal.subtitle: Apollo 13's two spaceships, joined nose to nose

stats.label: Command Module 'Odyssey'
stats.value: Home for the three astronauts, with the heat shield for coming home

stats.label: Service Module
stats.value: The main engine, oxygen tanks, fuel cells and power

stats.label: Lunar Module 'Aquarius'
stats.value: Built to carry two astronauts down to the Moon

stackReveal.line: Here are Odyssey and Aquarius, docked together. Remember the oxygen tanks inside the service module: they will matter very soon!

intro: Apollo 13 rides a giant Saturn V rocket up to orbit. Its engines need to burn for just the right time. Watch out: something unexpected is about to happen!
stageBurn.engineOut: The centre engine shut down early! It was shaking too much. Keep the other four burning longer!
stageBurn.over: A little too fast! Try to let go inside the green zone.
stageBurn.stage2Done: The four engines burned 34 seconds longer than planned to make up for it. Stage 2 drops away!
stageBurn.stage3Intro: Now the third stage takes over. Hold BURN again, and let go in the green zone!
stageBurn.stage3Done: In orbit! The third stage burned 9 seconds longer, and Apollo 13 was right on track.
stageBurn.resultText: Rockets carry extra fuel so they can fix surprises like this one. Apollo 13 was back on track and heading for the Moon...

task.title: Hold BURN!
task.help: Let go when the speed bar reaches the green zone.

stageBurn.tooSoon: Not fast enough yet! Hold BURN again.

slides.heading: A routine job
slides.text: Almost 56 hours after launch, more than 300,000 km (about 200,000 miles) from Earth, Mission Control asked Jack Swigert to stir the oxygen tanks. It was a normal job that kept the gauges accurate.

slides.heading: BANG!
slides.text: Seconds later, the crew heard a loud bang and the spaceship shook. Oxygen tank number 2 had exploded, and it damaged tank number 1 too.

slides.heading: "Houston, we've had a problem."
slides.text: Jack Swigert radioed: 'Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here.' Jim Lovell repeated it: 'Houston, we've had a problem.' In Mission Control, warning lights started flashing.
slides.speak: Jack Swigert radioed: Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here. Jim Lovell repeated it: Houston, we've had a problem. In Mission Control, warning lights started flashing.

image.alt: Flight controllers at their consoles in Mission Control

slides.credit: Photo: NASA · Mission Control during the Apollo 13 emergency

slides.heading: Leaking away
slides.text: Looking out of the window, Jim Lovell saw gas spraying into space. It was their oxygen! Odyssey needed it for breathing and for making electricity.

slides.heading: Work the problem
slides.text: Flight Director Gene Kranz and his team had to work out what was happening, fast. Let's help them read the gauges!

intro: Mission Control is full of gauges. Most still read normally, but some show big trouble! Let's find out what went wrong.
diagnose.panelHint: Tap a gauge to check it.

gauges.name: Oxygen tank 2
gauges.why: It reads zero! Tank 2 exploded and all of its oxygen is gone.

gauges.name: Oxygen tank 1
gauges.why: It is dropping fast. Tank 1 was damaged by the explosion and is leaking.

gauges.name: Hydrogen tanks
gauges.why: The hydrogen is fine. The trouble is with the oxygen.

gauges.name: Cabin pressure
gauges.why: The cabin is fine. The leak is outside it, in the service module.

gauges.name: Water
gauges.why: There is enough water for now.

gauges.name: Fuel cell 1
gauges.why: Dead! Fuel cells make electricity from oxygen and hydrogen. No oxygen, no electricity.

gauges.name: Fuel cell 2
gauges.why: Still working, for now. It runs on the oxygen leaking out of tank 1.

gauges.name: Fuel cell 3
gauges.why: Dead too. Two of Odyssey's three power makers have stopped.

gauges.name: Power line A
gauges.why: Still OK, powered by the last working fuel cell.

gauges.name: Power line B
gauges.why: Low voltage! The power supply to half of Odyssey's equipment has dropped.

diagnose.doneLine: You found every problem! The oxygen is leaking away and the fuel cells are dying, so Odyssey will soon run out of power. The crew must move into Aquarius and use it as a lifeboat!
diagnose.resultText: Reading the gauges told Mission Control exactly what was wrong. Next: the lifeboat plan.

task.title: Find the 5 broken gauges!
task.help: Tap gauges that read zero, drop fast or flash red.

intro: Odyssey is running out of power! The crew must move into Aquarius, the lunar module, and use it as a lifeboat. Be quick: Odyssey's power is draining away.
lifeboat.copyDone: Copied! Jim Lovell really worked out these numbers by hand, with a pencil.

items.name: The crew
items.info: Three astronauts in a lander built for two.

items.name: Food
items.info: Packed meals. The crew ate very little, because it was so cold.

items.name: Drinking water
items.info: Water was very short. The crew drank as little as they could.

items.name: Square air filters
items.info: Odyssey's square carbon dioxide filters. They'll be very important later!

items.name: Flashlights
items.info: With most lights switched off, flashlights helped the crew see.

items.name: Heat shield
items.why: The heat shield is part of Odyssey. It has to stay there to protect the crew on the way home!

items.name: Parachutes
items.why: Odyssey's parachutes stay packed in Odyssey, ready for splashdown.

items.name: Moon rock boxes
items.why: There won't be a Moon landing now, so the rock boxes can stay behind.

lifeboat.outOfPower: Odyssey's power ran very low! Hurry, power it down now.
lifeboat.doneLine: Odyssey is asleep and Aquarius is now a lifeboat. But Aquarius was built for two people for about two days, and now it must keep three people alive for about four days!
lifeboat.resultText: Odyssey's batteries are saved for re-entry. Now Aquarius has to make its power last...

copyTask.title: Copy the numbers!
copyTask.help: Drag each number into the box with the same name.

moveTask.title: Move to Aquarius!
moveTask.help: Drag the things the crew needs into Aquarius.

offTask.title: Power down Odyssey!
offTask.help: Press the red button to save its batteries for the trip home.

intro: Aquarius's batteries must last all the way home: about 90 hours! With everything switched on, they would run out much sooner.
The switches with a gold border keep the crew alive. Leave those on!

systems.name: Radio to Houston
systems.offWarn: Without the radio, the crew can't hear Mission Control's plan to get them home!

systems.name: Oxygen & air fans
systems.offWarn: Without fresh oxygen flowing, the crew can't breathe!

systems.name: Air filter fans
systems.offWarn: These fans push the air through the filters that clean out carbon dioxide. Keep them on!

systems.name: Guidance computer
systems.fact: Off! It was switched on only when the engine had to fire.

systems.name: Cabin heaters
systems.fact: Off. It got as cold as a fridge inside: about 3 °C (38 °F).

systems.name: Cabin lights
systems.fact: Off. The crew used flashlights instead.

systems.name: Rendezvous radar
systems.fact: Off. It was meant for meeting up with Odyssey after the Moon landing.

systems.name: Landing radar
systems.fact: Off. There would be no landing now.

systems.name: TV camera
systems.fact: Off. No TV shows on the way home!

systems.name: Window heaters
systems.fact: Off. The windows fogged up and frosted over.

systems.name: Panel displays
systems.fact: Mostly off. Only the most important gauges stayed lit.

powerDown.notEnough: Not enough power to get home yet! Switch off more things.
powerDown.doneLine: That's enough power to get home! The crew switched off almost everything. It was cold, dark and damp, but they were alive.
powerDown.resultText: With almost everything switched off, Aquarius's batteries could last all the way back to Earth.

task.title: Switch things off!
task.help: Turn off what the crew can live without, until the battery reaches the green line.

intro: The crew can't just turn around: they're moving much too fast! The plan is to swing around the Moon and let its gravity throw them back towards Earth.
freeReturn.hitMoon: That path hits the Moon! Keep sliding.
freeReturn.lost: That path flies off into space! Keep sliding.
freeReturn.missEarth: So close! The path must come back to the green zone at Earth.
freeReturn.secondEarly: A bit early! Wait until the ship reaches the yellow circle.
freeReturn.secondGood: Perfect timing! That burn made the trip home about 10 hours shorter.
freeReturn.resultText: This path is called a free return: it uses the Moon's gravity like a slingshot. The real burns used Aquarius's landing engine.

aimTask.title: Aim for home!
aimTask.help: Slide to aim. Make the dotted path loop around the Moon and back to the green zone.

flyTask.title: Swinging around the Moon...
flyTask.help: Get ready for one more burn after the Moon.

burn2Task.title: Burn again at the yellow circle!
burn2Task.help: Press BURN when the ship reaches the yellow circle. It gets the crew home sooner.

freeReturn.goodPath: That's it! The Moon's gravity will swing Apollo 13 home. Press BURN!

slides.heading: Behind the Moon
slides.text: Apollo 13 swung around the far side of the Moon, about 254 km (158 miles) above the surface. For a while the radio went quiet, because the Moon was in the way.

image.alt: Craters on the far side of the Moon

slides.credit: Photo: NASA · The Moon's far side, taken by the Apollo 13 crew

slides.heading: A record!
slides.text: About 400,171 km (248,655 miles) from Earth, the Apollo 13 crew became the people farthest from home ever. Their record lasted 56 years, until the Artemis II crew flew even farther in April 2026.

slides.heading: The Moon from Apollo 13
slides.text: The crew took photos of the Moon as they headed back towards Earth. It was as close as they would get.

image.alt: A nearly full Moon photographed from Apollo 13

slides.credit: Photo: NASA · The Moon, seen from Apollo 13 on the way home

slides.heading: Cold, wet and tired
slides.text: To save power, almost everything stayed off. The cabin was as cold as a fridge, water dripped down the walls, and the crew could hardly sleep.

slides.heading: A new danger
slides.text: Then another problem: the air was filling up with carbon dioxide, the gas we breathe out. Aquarius's air filters were never meant for three people for so long...

intro: Carbon dioxide is building up! Aquarius's round air filters are used up, and Odyssey's spare filters are square. They don't fit!
Engineers on Earth invented a fix using only things on board. Follow their steps, one at a time, before the meter reaches the red zone!

steps.text: Take a square filter from Odyssey.
Add cardboard to hold the shape.
Wrap it in a plastic bag.

items.name: Round filter
items.why: Those are Aquarius's own round filters, and they're already used up.

items.name: Spoon
items.why: A spoon can't make an airtight seal!

items.name: Camera
items.why: Great for photos, but no help with the air.

scrubber.wrongStep: Not yet! Follow the instructions in order.
scrubber.doneLine: It worked! The carbon dioxide level started to drop. The crew called it the 'mailbox'. This is the real one, on board Aquarius!

photo.alt: The real taped-up air filter on board Apollo 13
photo.credit: Photo: NASA · The 'mailbox' on board Aquarius

scrubber.resultText: Engineers on the ground built and tested the fix first, then read the instructions to the crew over the radio. Teamwork across 300,000 km!
scrubber.dragHelp: Drag it onto the filter on the bench.

intro: To get home safely, the engine must fire for exactly 14 seconds. But the guidance computer is off to save power!
So the crew steered by looking out of the window at Earth. Ready?
manualBurn.tooWobbly: It wobbled too much! Let's try that burn again.
manualBurn.resultText: Jim Lovell and Fred Haise shared the controls while Jack Swigert timed the burn. It worked perfectly!

task.title: Keep the line in the green band!
task.help: Use Up and Down to hold the line between day and night in the band.

intro: Almost home! But Odyssey has been cold and dark for days, and its batteries are low.
Engineers found a trick: send power backwards, from Aquarius to Odyssey!
powerUp.levelDone: Connected! Power is flowing into Odyssey.
powerUp.fact: Engineers and astronaut Ken Mattingly spent days in the simulator, writing a brand-new checklist so Odyssey could wake up using very little power.
powerUp.resultText: Odyssey's batteries were charged up, and the new checklist worked. The crew was ready to come home.

task.title: Connect the batteries!
task.help: Tap a cable piece to turn it. Make the power flow all the way to Odyssey.

slides.heading: Goodbye, service module
slides.text: Hours before landing, the crew let the service module go. As it drifted away, they finally saw the damage. Jim Lovell said: 'There's one whole side of that spacecraft missing!'
slides.speak: Hours before landing, the crew let the service module go. As it drifted away, they finally saw the damage. Jim Lovell said: There's one whole side of that spacecraft missing!

image.alt: The damaged service module, with one whole panel blown off

slides.credit: Photo: NASA · The damaged service module, photographed by the crew

slides.heading: Farewell, Aquarius
slides.text: About an hour before re-entry, the crew climbed back into Odyssey and let Aquarius go. Mission Control radioed: 'Farewell, Aquarius, and we thank you.'
slides.speak: About an hour before re-entry, the crew climbed back into Odyssey and let Aquarius go. Mission Control radioed: Farewell, Aquarius, and we thank you.

image.alt: The lunar module Aquarius floating away above Earth

slides.heading: Radio blackout
slides.text: Odyssey plunged into Earth's air, wrapped in glowing hot gas that blocks radio signals. The silence usually lasted about four minutes. This time, it went on much longer...

slides.heading: "Okay, Joe."
slides.text: At last, Jack Swigert's voice crackled through: 'Okay, Joe.' Odyssey had made it! Watch NASA's film of the splashdown, and Mission Control cheering.
slides.speak: At last, Jack Swigert's voice crackled through: Okay, Joe. Odyssey had made it! Watch NASA's film of the splashdown, and Mission Control cheering.

video.credit: Video: NASA · Apollo 13 splashdown and recovery (1970 film)

slides.heading: Splashdown!
slides.text: Odyssey splashed down safely in the South Pacific Ocean, close to the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima.

image.alt: The Apollo 13 capsule splashing into the ocean under three parachutes

slides.heading: Home safe
slides.text: Lovell, Swigert and Haise were cold, tired and hungry, but alive. All around the world, people cheered.

image.alt: The Apollo 13 crew stepping onto the deck of the USS Iwo Jima

slides.credit: Photo: NASA · The crew arrives on the USS Iwo Jima

slides.heading: A successful failure
slides.text: Apollo 13 never landed on the Moon. But thanks to teamwork, clever ideas and calm heads, everyone came home. Jim Lovell called it a 'successful failure'.

image.alt: People in Mission Control celebrating the safe splashdown

intro: After the flight, experts found out exactly what went wrong. It was not one big mistake: it was a chain of small problems, years apart!

cards.text: 1968: At the factory, the oxygen tank was dropped.
1970: In a test, its heater was left on for 8 hours.
The heater got far too hot and burnt the wires inside.
In space, the fans were switched on. A spark started a fire.
The tank burst and blew a panel off the spaceship!

investigation.wrongPlace: Not quite! Think about what had to happen first.
investigation.doneLine: That's the whole chain! NASA fixed every link: new switches, an extra oxygen tank, no fans inside the tanks and an extra battery. Apollo 14 flew safely to the Moon in 1971.
investigation.resultText: Engineers learn from every problem, so the next mission is safer.

task.title: Put the story in order!
task.help: Drag each picture to its spot, from the first problem to the explosion.

pages.say: Apollo 13 launched on April 11, 1970. An oxygen tank exploded on April 13, but the crew made it home safely on April 17.

pages.title: How the crew got home

items.name: Liftoff
items.text: April 11. A bumpy but safe ride to orbit.

items.name: Explosion
items.text: An oxygen tank bursts. Aquarius becomes a lifeboat.

items.name: Around the Moon
items.text: A free return, a record distance and the 'mailbox'.

pages.say: Day by day, the crew and Mission Control solved one problem after another, until Odyssey splashed down safely.

pages.title: What Apollo 13 taught us

items.name: Teamwork
items.text: Thousands of people on the ground solved problems in hours that would normally take weeks.

items.name: Safer spaceships
items.text: Later Apollo ships got an extra oxygen tank, an extra battery and safer wiring.

items.name: Practice and checklists
items.text: Hours in simulators helped engineers write brand-new checklists in just days.

items.name: Never give up
items.text: Even when things went wrong, everyone kept calm and kept working until the crew was home.

pages.say: Apollo 13 taught us about teamwork, careful engineering and practice, and about never giving up.

complete.title: Chapter 4 complete!
lines: You trained in the simulator and flew Apollo 13 to orbit.
You found the problem and moved the crew into the lifeboat.
You saved power, swung around the Moon and fixed the air.
You steered by the Earth, woke Odyssey up and solved the mystery.
complete.guide: What a rescue, star sailor! Next, let's ride along with Voyager 1 on a grand tour of the giant planets, and out into interstellar space.
